decks.title: 4-gons (Quadrilaterals): Part 1, types of 4-gon and the parallelogram
goals: Define a 4-gon and prove that its angles add up to 360 degrees
Name the types of 4-gon and say how they are related
Prove the properties of a parallelogram
Use the converses as tests for a parallelogram

slides.heading: Four sides, many shapes
slides.body_md: A book, a window, a kite in the sky: each has **four sides**. A figure with four sides is a **4-gon** (also called a quadrilateral). In this chapter we sort 4-gons into types and prove their properties.

visual.alt: Six kinds of four-sided figure, each with its name below: a trapezium with one pair of parallel sides marked with arrows, a parallelogram with two pairs of parallel sides, a rhombus with four equal sides, a rectangle with four right angles, a square with four equal sides and four right angles, and a kite with two pairs of equal adjacent sides.
visual.caption: Trapezium, parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle, square and kite.

slides.narration: Look around a classroom. The page of a book is a rectangle, a window frame is a rectangle too, and a kite flying outside has quite another shape. All of these have four sides. A figure with four sides is called a four-gon, or a quadrilateral. In this chapter we sort four sided figures into types, and we find out which properties each type has and why.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Define a **4-gon** and prove its **angle sum** is $360^\circ$
Name the types: **trapezium, parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle, square, kite**
Prove the **properties of a parallelogram**
Use the **converses** as tests

visual.alt: Flow of Part 1: what a 4-gon is and its angle sum, the types of 4-gon, the properties of a parallelogram, and the tests that show a 4-gon is a parallelogram.
visual.caption: Part 1 road map.

slides.narration: In this part we define a four-gon and its parts, and we prove that its angles add up to three hundred sixty degrees. We learn the names of the main types, and how they are related. Then we prove properties of a parallelogram, such as equal opposite sides and diagonals that bisect each other, and we learn the tests that tell us a four-gon is a parallelogram.

slides.heading: What is a 4-gon?
slides.body_md: A **4-gon** $ABCD$ has four **vertices** and four **sides** $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$, joined in order. Sides that meet are **adjacent**; sides that do not meet are **opposite**. A segment joining opposite vertices is a **diagonal**: $AC$ and $BD$.

visual.alt: A four-sided figure ABCD with its four vertices A, B, C and D in order, four sides AB, BC, CD and DA, and two dashed diagonals AC and BD that join opposite vertices.
visual.caption: A 4-gon has four vertices, four sides and two diagonals.

slides.narration: A four-gon has four vertices and four sides, joined in order. We name it by its vertices going round, like A B C D. Sides that meet at a vertex are adjacent, and sides that do not meet are opposite. A segment joining two opposite vertices is a diagonal, and a four-gon has two diagonals, which are dashed in the figure.

slides.heading: The angles of a 4-gon add up to 360 degrees
slides.body_md: The diagonal $AC$ splits $ABCD$ into two triangles, each with angle sum $180^\circ$. Together their angles make the four angles of the 4-gon, so the sum is $2 \times 180^\circ = 360^\circ$. Check: $80 + 95 + 70 + 115 = 360$.

visual.alt: A four-sided figure ABCD with angles of 80 degrees at A, 95 degrees at B, 70 degrees at C and 115 degrees at D. The dashed diagonal AC splits it into two triangles ABC and ACD.
visual.caption: The angles add up to $80^\circ + 95^\circ + 70^\circ + 115^\circ = 360^\circ$.

slides.narration: Draw the diagonal A C. It splits the four-gon into two triangles, A B C and A C D. The angles of each triangle add up to one hundred eighty degrees. The angles of the two triangles together make up exactly the four angles of the four-gon. So the angles of a four-gon add up to three hundred sixty degrees. In the figure, eighty, ninety-five, seventy and one hundred fifteen make three hundred sixty.

slides.heading: Types of 4-gon
slides.body_md: Each type is defined by **one** property. The other properties follow from it.

rows: At least one pair of parallel sides
The other two sides need not be parallel
Both pairs of opposite sides parallel
Opposite sides equal, opposite angles equal, diagonals bisect each other
A parallelogram with four equal sides
It is a parallelogram; the diagonals are equal
Four equal sides and four right angles
Both a rhombus and a rectangle
Two pairs of equal adjacent sides
Diagonals are perpendicular; one diagonal is a line of symmetry

visual.alt: Table of six types of 4-gon with their defining property and other properties: trapezium, parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle, square and kite.
visual.caption: Each type is defined by one property; the others follow from it.

slides.narration: Here are the main types. A trapezium has at least one pair of parallel sides. A parallelogram has both pairs of opposite sides parallel. A rhombus is a parallelogram with four equal sides, and a rectangle is a four-gon with four right angles. A square is both. A kite has two pairs of equal adjacent sides. Notice that every square is a rectangle, and every rectangle is a parallelogram.

slides.heading: How the types are related
slides.body_md: An arrow means "is a special case of". Every **square** is a rhombus and a rectangle; every **rhombus** and **rectangle** is a parallelogram; every **parallelogram** is a trapezium. A **kite** is not a parallelogram in general.

visual.alt: Chart of how the types of 4-gon are related: a trapezium is a special 4-gon, a parallelogram is a special trapezium, a rhombus and a rectangle are special parallelograms, a square is a special rhombus and a special rectangle, and a kite is a separate special 4-gon.
visual.caption: An arrow means "is a special case of".

slides.narration: This chart shows how the types are related. An arrow means is a special case of. A parallelogram is a special trapezium. A rhombus and a rectangle are special parallelograms, and a square is a special rhombus and a special rectangle. A kite is not a parallelogram in general, because its opposite sides are not parallel.

slides.heading: Quick check: name the type
slides.body_md: A 4-gon has two pairs of equal adjacent sides, but its opposite sides are not parallel. What is it?

visual.alt: Six kinds of four-sided figure, each with its name below: a trapezium with one pair of parallel sides marked with arrows, a parallelogram with two pairs of parallel sides, a rhombus with four equal sides, a rectangle with four right angles, a square with four equal sides and four right angles, and a kite with two pairs of equal adjacent sides.
visual.caption: Trapezium, parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle, square and kite.

slides.narration: Think about which type has equal adjacent sides.

slides.heading: The parallelogram and its diagonal
slides.body_md: In a **parallelogram** $AB \parallel DC$ and $AD \parallel BC$. The diagonal $AC$ makes **alternate angles** equal: $\angle DAC = \angle ACB$ and $\angle BAC = \angle ACD$.

visual.alt: A parallelogram ABCD with AB parallel to DC and AD parallel to BC, marked with arrows. The dashed diagonal AC makes two triangles. The alternate angles DAC and ACB have one arc each, and the alternate angles BAC and ACD have two arcs each.
visual.caption: The diagonal AC makes alternate angles equal: $\angle DAC = \angle ACB$ and $\angle BAC = \angle ACD$.

slides.narration: In a parallelogram both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, shown by the arrows. Draw the diagonal A C. Because A D is parallel to B C, the angles D A C and A C B are alternate angles and are equal. Because A B is parallel to D C, the angles B A C and A C D are alternate angles and are equal. These equal angles will help us prove the main properties.

slides.heading: Opposite sides and angles are equal
slides.body_md: **Theorem:** in a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal and opposite angles are equal. The proof uses the congruent triangles $ABC$ and $CDA$.

rows: $ABCD$ is a parallelogram: $AB \parallel DC$ and $AD \parallel BC$. Join the diagonal $AC$
$\angle A = \angle DAC + \angle BAC = \angle ACB + \angle ACD = \angle C$

visual.alt: Table: proof that opposite sides and opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal. Join the diagonal AC; the alternate angles DAC and ACB are equal and BAC and ACD are equal, AC is common, so triangles ABC and CDA are congruent by ASA. Then AB equals CD, BC equals DA and angle B equals angle D, and adding the equal angles at A and C gives angle A equals angle C.
visual.caption: The diagonal splits the parallelogram into two congruent triangles.

slides.narration: Theorem: in a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal and opposite angles are equal. The triangles A B C and C D A have two equal angles and the common side A C between them, so they are congruent by angle side angle. By corresponding parts, A B equals C D, and B C equals D A. Adding the two pairs of equal angles at A and C shows that the angle A equals the angle C.

slides.heading: The diagonals bisect each other
slides.body_md: **Theorem:** the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other. In $\triangle AOB$ and $\triangle COD$ two angles and the side between them are equal (ASA), so $OA = OC$ and $OB = OD$.

visual.alt: A parallelogram ABCD with diagonals AC and BD crossing at O. AO and OC carry one tick, BO and OD carry two ticks. The vertically opposite angles AOB and COD have one arc each, and the alternate angles OAB and OCD have two arcs each.
visual.caption: The diagonals meet at O with $AO = OC$ and $BO = OD$.

slides.narration: Theorem: the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other. Look at triangles A O B and C O D. The angles O A B and O C D are alternate angles, so they are equal. The angles O B A and O D C are alternate angles too. And A B equals C D, because opposite sides are equal. So the triangles are congruent by angle side angle, and O A equals O C, and O B equals O D.

slides.heading: The proof in steps
slides.body_md: The full proof, with a reason for every step. Check: in the figure $AB = 7$ cm.

rows: In $\triangle AOB$ and $\triangle COD$: $\angle OAB = \angle OCD$
$AB = 7$ cm and $AO = OC \approx 4.66$ cm in the figure

visual.alt: Table: proof that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other. In triangles AOB and COD the alternate angles OAB and OCD are equal, AB equals CD, and the alternate angles OBA and ODC are equal, so the triangles are congruent by ASA and OA equals OC and OB equals OD.
visual.caption: The triangles AOB and COD are congruent.

slides.narration: Here is the proof written step by step. First the alternate angles at A and C are equal, because A B is parallel to D C. Then A B equals C D, as opposite sides of a parallelogram. The alternate angles at B and D are equal. Angle side angle then gives congruent triangles, and the corresponding parts O A and O C are equal, and so are O B and O D.

slides.heading: Quick check: the diagonals
slides.body_md: In a parallelogram $ABCD$ the diagonals meet at $O$ and $OA = 6.5$ cm. How long is the diagonal $AC$?

visual.alt: A parallelogram ABCD with diagonals AC and BD crossing at O. AO and OC carry one tick, BO and OD carry two ticks. The vertically opposite angles AOB and COD have one arc each, and the alternate angles OAB and OCD have two arcs each.
visual.caption: The diagonals meet at O with $AO = OC$ and $BO = OD$.

slides.narration: Remember that the diagonals bisect each other.

slides.heading: The converses: tests for a parallelogram
slides.body_md: Each property has a **converse**, and the converses are true. They give **tests** that show a 4-gon is a parallelogram. But **one** pair of equal opposite sides is **not** enough.

rows: Both pairs of opposite sides equal
A diagonal makes two congruent triangles (SSS), so alternate angles are equal
Both pairs of opposite angles equal
The angles add up to $360^\circ$, so $\angle A + \angle B = 180^\circ$ and $AD \parallel BC$
Two pairs of congruent triangles (SAS), so alternate angles are equal
One pair of opposite sides equal and parallel
A diagonal makes two congruent triangles (SAS), so the other pair is parallel
Only one pair of opposite sides equal
An isosceles trapezium has equal legs but is not a parallelogram

visual.alt: Table of tests for a parallelogram: both pairs of opposite sides equal, both pairs of opposite angles equal, diagonals that bisect each other, and one pair of opposite sides equal and parallel all give a parallelogram; only one pair of opposite sides equal does not, as an isosceles trapezium shows.
visual.caption: The converses of the parallelogram properties are tests.

slides.narration: The converses are also true, and they give us tests. A four-gon is a parallelogram if both pairs of opposite sides are equal. It is a parallelogram if both pairs of opposite angles are equal. It is a parallelogram if its diagonals bisect each other. And it is a parallelogram if one pair of opposite sides is both equal and parallel. But one pair of equal opposite sides alone is not enough.

slides.heading: Rhombus, rectangle and square
slides.body_md: The diagonals of a **rhombus** are perpendicular: with diagonals $8$ cm and $6$ cm the side is $\sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5$ cm. The diagonals of a **rectangle** are equal: for $8$ cm by $6$ cm each is $10$ cm. A **square** has both properties.

visual.alt: Left: a rhombus ABCD with all sides 5 centimetres and diagonals of 8 and 6 centimetres that cross at O at a right angle. Right: a rectangle PQRS of 8 by 6 centimetres whose two diagonals PR and QS are both 10 centimetres.
visual.caption: The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular; the diagonals of a rectangle are equal.

slides.narration: Rhombus and rectangle have extra properties. The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular, and in the figure the diagonals of eight and six centimetres meet at right angles, so the side is five centimetres. The diagonals of a rectangle are equal, and for a rectangle of eight by six centimetres each diagonal is ten centimetres. A square has both properties.

slides.heading: Which property for which type?
slides.body_md: A table to compare the four special 4-gons. Every row is checked on a drawing.

visual.alt: Table comparing a parallelogram, a rhombus, a rectangle and a square: all have opposite sides equal and diagonals that bisect each other; diagonals are equal for a rectangle and a square; diagonals are perpendicular for a rhombus and a square; four equal sides for a rhombus and a square; four right angles for a rectangle and a square.
visual.caption: Which properties hold for which type.

slides.narration: This table compares a parallelogram, a rhombus, a rectangle and a square. All four have equal opposite sides and diagonals that bisect each other. The diagonals are equal for a rectangle and a square. The diagonals are perpendicular for a rhombus and a square. A rhombus and a square have four equal sides, and a rectangle and a square have four right angles.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: angles of a parallelogram
slides.body_md: In a parallelogram $ABCD$, $\angle A = (2x + 20)^\circ$ and $\angle B = (3x - 10)^\circ$. Find $x$ and all four angles.
bullets: **Adjacent angles —** they add up to $180^\circ$: $5x + 10 = 180$, so $x = 34$
**$\angle A$ and $\angle B$ —** $88^\circ$ and $92^\circ$
**Opposite angles are equal —** $\angle C = 88^\circ$, $\angle D = 92^\circ$

visual.alt: A parallelogram ABCD. The angle at A is marked 2x plus 20 degrees and the adjacent angle at B is marked 3x minus 10 degrees.
visual.caption: Adjacent angles of a parallelogram add up to $180^\circ$.

slides.narration: In a parallelogram A B C D the angle A is two x plus twenty and the angle B is three x minus ten degrees. Adjacent angles of a parallelogram add up to one hundred eighty degrees. So five x plus ten equals one hundred eighty, and x is thirty-four. The angle A is eighty-eight degrees, the angle B is ninety-two degrees, and the opposite angles are equal to these.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a 4-gon whose diagonals bisect each other
slides.body_md: In a 4-gon $ABCD$ the diagonals meet at $O$, with $OA = OC = 3.5$ cm and $OB = OD = 2.5$ cm. Prove that $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.
bullets: **Vertically opposite angles —** $\angle AOB = \angle COD$
**SAS —** $\triangle AOB \cong \triangle COD$, so $\angle OAB = \angle OCD$ and $AB \parallel DC$
**Same for the other pair —** $AD \parallel BC$, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram

visual.alt: A four-sided figure ABCD whose diagonals AC and BD cross at O. OA and OC are both 3.5 centimetres, OB and OD are both 2.5 centimetres, and the angle COB is 70 degrees. The task is to show that ABCD is a parallelogram.
visual.caption: The diagonals bisect each other.

slides.narration: In a four-gon A B C D the diagonals meet at O, with O A equal to O C, and O B equal to O D. The angles A O B and C O D are vertically opposite, so the triangles A O B and C O D are congruent by side angle side. So the alternate angles O A B and O C D are equal, and A B is parallel to D C. In the same way A D is parallel to B C.

slides.heading: Quick check: not enough
slides.body_md: Which condition does **not** guarantee that a 4-gon is a parallelogram?

rows: Both pairs of opposite sides equal
A diagonal makes two congruent triangles (SSS), so alternate angles are equal
Both pairs of opposite angles equal
The angles add up to $360^\circ$, so $\angle A + \angle B = 180^\circ$ and $AD \parallel BC$
Two pairs of congruent triangles (SAS), so alternate angles are equal
One pair of opposite sides equal and parallel
A diagonal makes two congruent triangles (SAS), so the other pair is parallel
Only one pair of opposite sides equal
An isosceles trapezium has equal legs but is not a parallelogram

visual.alt: Table of tests for a parallelogram: both pairs of opposite sides equal, both pairs of opposite angles equal, diagonals that bisect each other, and one pair of opposite sides equal and parallel all give a parallelogram; only one pair of opposite sides equal does not, as an isosceles trapezium shows.
visual.caption: The converses of the parallelogram properties are tests.

slides.narration: Recall the isosceles trapezium.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: A **4-gon** has four vertices, four sides and two diagonals; its angles add up to $360^\circ$
**Types:** trapezium, parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle, square, kite; a square is a rhombus and a rectangle
In a **parallelogram** opposite sides and angles are equal and the diagonals bisect each other
**Tests:** both pairs of opposite sides equal, both pairs of opposite angles equal, diagonals bisect each other, or one pair of opposite sides equal and parallel

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: the angles of a 4-gon add up to 360 degrees, the types of 4-gon from trapezium to square, the properties of a parallelogram, and the converses used as tests.
visual.caption: The story of Part 1.

slides.narration: To sum up. A four-gon has four vertices, four sides and two diagonals, and its angles add up to three hundred sixty degrees. The types are trapezium, parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle, square and kite. In a parallelogram opposite sides and opposite angles are equal and the diagonals bisect each other. The converses give tests that show a four-gon is a parallelogram.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Proofs (3 marks):** draw the diagonal, show the congruent triangles with reasons, then use CPCT
**Angle problems (2 marks):** write the equation from the property, solve, then state all angles
**Mistake:** saying a 4-gon is a parallelogram because one pair of opposite sides is equal
**Mistake:** mixing up the diagonal properties of a rhombus and a rectangle

visual.alt: Table comparing a parallelogram, a rhombus, a rectangle and a square: all have opposite sides equal and diagonals that bisect each other; diagonals are equal for a rectangle and a square; diagonals are perpendicular for a rhombus and a square; four equal sides for a rhombus and a square; four right angles for a rectangle and a square.
visual.caption: Which properties hold for which type.

slides.narration: In proofs, draw the diagonal, show the congruent triangles with a reason for each pair of equal parts, and then use corresponding parts. In angle problems, write an equation from the property, solve it, and state all the angles. Two common slips are saying a four-gon is a parallelogram because only one pair of opposite sides is equal, and mixing up the diagonal properties of a rhombus and a rectangle.

decks.title: 4-gons (Quadrilaterals): Part 2, midpoints, medians, symmetry and tiling
goals: Prove the midpoint theorem and its converse
Prove that the medians of a triangle are concurrent
Prove that the midpoints of the sides of a 4-gon form a parallelogram
Describe the symmetry of 4-gons and explain why every 4-gon tiles the plane

slides.heading: A line joining two midpoints
slides.body_md: A beam fixed halfway up each slanting side of a gable looks **parallel** to the bottom, and **half as long**. This is the **midpoint theorem**, and it unlocks many results about 4-gons.

visual.alt: A triangle ABC with D the midpoint of AB and E the midpoint of AC. The segment DE is parallel to BC, marked with arrows, and is 4 centimetres while BC is 8 centimetres.
visual.caption: The segment joining the midpoints of two sides is parallel to the third side and half as long.

slides.narration: A line that joins the midpoints of two sides of a triangle has a lovely property. Imagine the gable end of a roof, with a beam fixed halfway up each slanting side. The beam looks parallel to the bottom, and half as long. In this part we prove it, and we use it to show that the medians of a triangle meet at a point, and that the midpoints of any four-gon form a parallelogram.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Prove the **midpoint theorem** and its **converse**
Prove that the **medians** of a triangle are concurrent
Prove that joining the **midpoints** of a 4-gon gives a parallelogram
Describe **symmetry** and **tiling** of 4-gons

visual.alt: Flow of Part 2: the midpoint theorem and its converse, the concurrency of the medians, the parallelogram formed by the midpoints of a 4-gon, and symmetry and tiling.
visual.caption: Part 2 road map.

slides.narration: First the midpoint theorem and its converse. Then the medians of a triangle, which turn out to be concurrent. Then the parallelogram that appears inside any four-gon when we join the midpoints of its sides. We finish with symmetry, which means reflection and rotation of four-gons, and with tiling, which explains why every four-gon can cover a floor.

slides.heading: The midpoint theorem
slides.body_md: **Theorem:** the segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is **parallel** to the third side and **half** as long. Here $DE \parallel BC$ and $DE = \frac12 BC = 4$ cm.

visual.alt: A triangle ABC with D the midpoint of AB and E the midpoint of AC. The segment DE is parallel to BC, marked with arrows, and is 4 centimetres while BC is 8 centimetres.
visual.caption: The segment joining the midpoints of two sides is parallel to the third side and half as long.

slides.narration: The midpoint theorem says: the segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side, and is half as long. In the figure D and E are midpoints of A B and A C. The segment D E is four centimetres and parallel to B C, which is eight centimetres.

slides.heading: Proof of the midpoint theorem
slides.body_md: Extend $DE$ to $F$ with $EF = DE$ and join $CF$. The proof builds a **parallelogram** $BDFC$.

rows: $D$, $E$ are midpoints of $AB$, $AC$. Extend $DE$ to $F$ so that $EF = DE$ and join $CF$
CPCT; alternate angles $\angle ADE = \angle CFE$ are equal
One pair of opposite sides ($BD$ and $CF$) equal and parallel
$DE = 4$ cm and $BC = 8$ cm in the figure

visual.alt: Table: proof of the midpoint theorem. Extend DE to F with EF equal to DE and join CF. Triangles AED and CEF are congruent by SAS, so CF equals AD which equals BD, and CF is parallel to AB. So BDFC is a parallelogram, DF is parallel and equal to BC, and DE is half of DF.
visual.caption: The proof builds a parallelogram.

slides.narration: To prove it, extend D E to F so that E F equals D E, and join C F. Triangles A E D and C E F are congruent by side angle side, because the angles at E are vertically opposite. So C F equals B D and is parallel to it, which makes B D F C a parallelogram. Then D F is parallel and equal to B C, and D E is half of D F.

slides.heading: Quick check: midpoint theorem
slides.body_md: In triangle $ABC$, $D$ and $E$ are the midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$, and $BC = 14$ cm. What is $DE$?

visual.alt: A triangle ABC with D the midpoint of AB and E the midpoint of AC. The segment DE is parallel to BC, marked with arrows, and is 4 centimetres while BC is 8 centimetres.
visual.caption: The segment joining the midpoints of two sides is parallel to the third side and half as long.

slides.narration: Use the midpoint theorem.

slides.heading: The converse of the midpoint theorem
slides.body_md: **Converse:** a line through the **midpoint** of one side of a triangle, **parallel** to a second side, **bisects** the third side. $D$ is the midpoint of $AB$ and $DE \parallel BC$, so $AE = EC$.

visual.alt: A triangle ABC with D the midpoint of AB. A line through D parallel to BC, marked with arrows, meets AC at E. The segments AE and EC are marked with question marks: they should be equal.
visual.caption: A line through the midpoint of one side, parallel to a second side, bisects the third side.

slides.narration: The converse says: a line through the midpoint of one side of a triangle, parallel to a second side, bisects the third side. Here D is the midpoint of A B, and D E is parallel to B C. Let E prime be the midpoint of A C. By the midpoint theorem, D E prime is also parallel to B C. Only one line through D is parallel to B C, so E is E prime, and A E equals E C.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: joining the midpoints
slides.body_md: The sides of $\triangle ABC$ are $AB = 10$ cm, $BC = 12$ cm and $CA = 14$ cm. $D$, $E$, $F$ are the midpoints of $BC$, $CA$, $AB$. Find the sides and perimeter of $\triangle DEF$.
bullets: **Midpoint theorem —** $EF = \frac12 BC = 6$, $FD = \frac12 CA = 7$, $DE = \frac12 AB = 5$ cm
**Perimeter —** $6 + 7 + 5 = 18$ cm, half of $36$ cm
**The four small triangles —** each has sides $5$, $6$, $7$ cm, so they are congruent (SSS)

visual.alt: A triangle ABC with sides AB of 10, BC of 12 and CA of 14 centimetres. D, E and F are the midpoints of BC, CA and AB, and the dashed triangle DEF inside has sides EF of 6, FD of 7 and DE of 5 centimetres, each half of a side of ABC and parallel to it.
visual.caption: Joining the midpoints of the sides gives a triangle with half-size sides.

slides.narration: The sides of a triangle are ten, twelve and fourteen centimetres. The midpoints of its sides are joined. By the midpoint theorem each side of the new triangle is half of a side of the old one and parallel to it. So the new sides are five, six and seven centimetres, and the perimeter is eighteen centimetres, half of thirty-six. The four small triangles are congruent by side side side.

slides.heading: Medians are concurrent
slides.body_md: A **median** joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. The three medians $AD$, $BE$, $CF$ pass through one point $G$ (**concurrent**), the **centroid**. $G$ divides each median in the ratio $2 : 1$, the longer part towards the vertex.

visual.alt: A triangle ABC with D, E and F the midpoints of BC, CA and AB, marked with ticks. The three dashed medians AD, BE and CF all pass through one point G.
visual.caption: The three medians meet at the centroid $G$.

slides.narration: A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. A triangle has three medians. In the figure the medians A D, B E and C F all pass through one point G. Lines that pass through one point are called concurrent. The point G is called the centroid, and it divides each median in the ratio two to one, with the longer part next to the vertex.

slides.heading: Why the medians meet in one point
slides.body_md: The proof applies the midpoint theorem to $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle GBC$.

rows: The medians $BE$ and $CF$ meet at $G$. $P$, $Q$ are the midpoints of $GB$, $GC$
$FE \parallel PQ$ and $FE = PQ$, so $FEQP$ is a parallelogram
One pair of opposite sides equal and parallel
The diagonals $EP$ and $FQ$ bisect each other at $G$, so $EG = GP$
They lie along the medians $BE$ and $CF$, which meet at $G$
$BG = 2 \times GP = 2 \times GE$, and in the same way $CG = 2 \times GF$

slides.heading: The midpoints of any 4-gon
slides.body_md: Join the midpoints $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ of the sides of **any** 4-gon $ABCD$. Then $PQRS$ is always a **parallelogram**. Each side of $PQRS$ is parallel to a diagonal of $ABCD$.

In the figure the sides of P Q R S are marked with ticks, and the opposite sides have the same ticks. The dashed diagonals A C and B D explain why: each side of P Q R S is parallel to a diagonal.

A pair of opposite sides that is equal and parallel makes P Q R S a parallelogram.

Since the diagonals are perpendicular, the sides of P Q R S are perpendicular too, so it is a rectangle. Its perimeter is sixteen centimetres and its area is fifteen square centimetres.

slides.heading: Lines of symmetry
slides.body_md: A **line of symmetry** is a line such that folding along it makes the two halves fit exactly. A **rectangle** has $2$, a **rhombus** has $2$ (along its diagonals), a **kite** has $1$. A general parallelogram has none, and a square has $4$.

visual.alt: Three four-sided figures with their lines of symmetry drawn as dashed lines: a rectangle with two lines of symmetry joining midpoints of opposite sides, a rhombus with two lines of symmetry along its diagonals, and a kite with one line of symmetry along its longer diagonal.
visual.caption: A rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry, a rhombus 2 and a kite 1.

slides.narration: A figure has a line of symmetry if folding along the line makes the two halves fit exactly. A rectangle has two lines of symmetry, through the midpoints of opposite sides. A rhombus has two, along its diagonals. A kite has one, along its longer diagonal. A general parallelogram has none, and a square has four.

slides.heading: Rotational symmetry
slides.body_md: A figure has **rotational symmetry** if a turn about a point, by less than a full turn, makes it fit itself. The **order** is how many times it fits in one full turn. A **parallelogram** has order $2$ (half-turn about the centre), a **square** has order $4$ (quarter-turn).

visual.alt: Left: a square ABCD with its centre O. The turns from OA to OB to OC to OD are right angles, so a quarter-turn about O maps the square onto itself. Right: a parallelogram PQRS with its centre M, where the angle PMR is a straight angle of 180 degrees, so a half-turn about M maps the parallelogram onto itself.
visual.caption: The square has rotational symmetry of order 4, the parallelogram of order 2.

slides.narration: A figure has rotational symmetry if a turn about a point, by less than a full turn, makes it fit itself. A parallelogram fits itself after a half turn about the point where the diagonals meet, so its order of rotation is two. A square fits itself after a quarter turn, so its order is four. A kite has order one, meaning only the full turn.

slides.heading: Why every 4-gon tiles the plane
slides.body_md: Place four copies of the same 4-gon around a point, using each of its four angles once: $80 + 115 + 70 + 95 = 360$. A full turn means **no gap**, so the corners fit. This works for **every** 4-gon because its angles always add up to $360^\circ$.

visual.alt: Four copies of the same four-sided figure, with angles of 80, 95, 70 and 115 degrees, meet at a point O. Each copy has a different one of its angles at O, and together the angles 80, 115, 70 and 95 fill the whole turn of 360 degrees around O, with no gap and no overlap.
visual.caption: Four copies of the 4-gon fit around a point: $80^\circ + 115^\circ + 70^\circ + 95^\circ = 360^\circ$.

slides.narration: Why can every four-gon cover a floor with no gaps? Place four copies of the same four-gon round a point, one corner from each, using the four different angles. Here the angles are eighty, ninety-five, seventy and one hundred fifteen degrees. They add up to three hundred sixty degrees, which is a full turn, so the corners fit with no gap. This works for any four-gon.

slides.heading: Quick check: tiling
slides.body_md: Three angles of a 4-gon tile are $75^\circ$, $105^\circ$ and $85^\circ$. What must the fourth angle be?

rows: A full turn: no gap and no overlap

visual.caption: The angle sum of a 4-gon is a full turn.

slides.narration: The four angles of a four-gon add up to a full turn.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: **Midpoint theorem:** the segment joining two midpoints is parallel to the third side and half as long; its **converse** also holds
The **medians** of a triangle meet at the **centroid**, which divides each median in the ratio $2 : 1$
The midpoints of the sides of **any** 4-gon form a **parallelogram** (Varignon)
**Symmetry:** rectangle 2 lines, rhombus 2, kite 1, square 4; parallelogram has rotational order 2
**Tiling:** every 4-gon tiles the plane because its angles add up to $360^\circ$

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 2: the midpoint theorem and its converse, the medians meeting in a point and dividing each other in the ratio 2 to 1, the midpoint 4-gon being a parallelogram, and symmetry and tiling.
visual.caption: The story of Part 2.

slides.narration: To sum up. The segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half as long, and the converse also holds. The medians of a triangle meet at the centroid, which divides each median in the ratio two to one. The midpoints of the sides of any four-gon form a parallelogram. Every four-gon tiles the plane, because its angles add up to three hundred sixty degrees.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Midpoint theorem proofs (3 marks):** the construction, the congruent triangles with reasons, then the conclusion
**Numerical questions (2 marks):** name the theorem, then halve the right side
**Symmetry (1–2 marks):** count lines of symmetry and the order of rotation
**Mistake:** applying the midpoint theorem when the points are not midpoints

visual.caption: Counted by testing every reflection and rotation on the drawn shapes.

slides.narration: In proofs of the midpoint theorem, write the construction, show the congruent triangles with a reason for each pair of equal parts, and then state the conclusion. In numerical questions, name the theorem and then halve the correct side. In symmetry questions, count the lines of symmetry and the order of rotation. A common slip is using the midpoint theorem when the points are not midpoints.

sections.heading: 1. Definition and angle sum
sections.body_md: A **4-gon** (quadrilateral) $ABCD$ has four vertices, four sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$ and two diagonals $AC$, $BD$. A diagonal that lies inside splits it into two triangles, so the **sum of its angles is $360^\circ$**. Opposite sides do not meet; adjacent sides do.

A segment joining two opposite vertices.

sections.heading: 2. Types of 4-gon
sections.body_md: **Trapezium:** at least one pair of parallel sides. **Parallelogram:** both pairs of opposite sides parallel. **Rhombus:** a parallelogram with four equal sides. **Rectangle:** four right angles (it is a parallelogram). **Square:** four equal sides and four right angles (a rhombus and a rectangle). **Kite:** two pairs of equal adjacent sides. Every square is a rectangle and a rhombus; every rectangle and rhombus is a parallelogram; every parallelogram is a trapezium.

sections.heading: 3. Parallelogram: properties and tests
sections.body_md:
In a parallelogram: **opposite sides are equal**, **opposite angles are equal**, **adjacent angles add up to $180^\circ$** and **the diagonals bisect each other**. The proofs use the diagonal and alternate angles to get congruent triangles (ASA).

**Tests (the converses):** a 4-gon is a parallelogram if (i) both pairs of opposite sides are equal, or (ii) both pairs of opposite angles are equal, or (iii) its diagonals bisect each other, or (iv) one pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel. One pair of equal opposite sides alone is not enough (isosceles trapezium).

In a **rhombus** the diagonals are perpendicular; in a **rectangle** they are equal; a square has both.

sections.heading: 4. The midpoint theorem and its converse
sections.body_md:
**Theorem:** the segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is **parallel** to the third side and **half** of it: $DE \parallel BC$, $DE = \frac12 BC$.

*Proof idea:* extend $DE$ to $F$ with $EF = DE$; $\triangle AED \cong \triangle CEF$ (SAS), so $BDFC$ is a parallelogram.

**Converse:** a line through the midpoint of one side, parallel to a second side, bisects the third side (uniqueness of the parallel line through a point).

Joining the three midpoints gives a triangle with half-size sides, so its perimeter is half.

sections.heading: 5. Medians and the Varignon parallelogram
sections.body_md:
A **median** joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. The three medians are **concurrent**, at the **centroid** $G$, which divides each median in the ratio $2 : 1$ ($AG = 2\,GD$). *Proof idea:* in $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle GBC$ the midpoint theorem gives a parallelogram $FEQP$ whose diagonals lie along the medians and bisect each other at $G$.

**Varignon:** the midpoints $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ of the sides of **any** 4-gon form a parallelogram, with sides parallel to the diagonals and half as long. It is a rectangle if the diagonals are perpendicular, a rhombus if they are equal, and a square if both. Its area is half the area of $ABCD$.

sections.heading: 6. Symmetry and tiling
sections.body_md:
A **line of symmetry** folds a figure onto itself. A figure has **rotational symmetry** of order $n$ if a turn of $360^\circ \div n$ about a point makes it fit itself. Rectangle: $2$ lines, order $2$. Rhombus: $2$ lines, order $2$. Square: $4$ lines, order $4$. Parallelogram: no lines, order $2$. Kite: $1$ line, order $1$.

**Tiling:** four copies of any 4-gon can meet at a point, using each of its four angles once, because the angles add up to $360^\circ$. So every 4-gon tiles the plane with no gaps and no overlaps.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Proofs (3 marks):* construction, congruent triangles with reasons, conclusion.
- *Numerical questions (2 marks):* name the theorem, then use it.
- *Symmetry (1–2 marks):* lines of symmetry and order of rotation.

**Common mistakes**
1. Calling a 4-gon a parallelogram because one pair of opposite sides is equal.
2. Mixing up the diagonals of a rhombus (perpendicular) and a rectangle (equal).
3. Using the midpoint theorem when the points are not midpoints.
4. Forgetting the ratio $2 : 1$ is measured from the vertex.
5. Forgetting reasons beside the steps of a proof.

cards.front_md: What is a 4-gon?
cards.back_md: A closed figure made of four line segments joined end to end (a quadrilateral).

cards.front_md: What is a diagonal of a 4-gon?
cards.back_md: A segment joining two opposite vertices.

cards.front_md: What is the sum of the angles of a 4-gon?
Why do the angles of a 4-gon add up to $360^\circ$?
cards.back_md: A diagonal splits it into two triangles, each with angle sum $180^\circ$.

cards.front_md: What is a trapezium?
cards.back_md: A 4-gon with at least one pair of parallel sides.

cards.front_md: What is a parallelogram?
cards.back_md: A 4-gon with both pairs of opposite sides parallel.

cards.front_md: What is a rhombus?
cards.back_md: A parallelogram with four equal sides.

cards.front_md: What is a rectangle?
cards.back_md: A 4-gon with four right angles (it is a parallelogram).

cards.front_md: What is a square?
cards.back_md: A 4-gon with four equal sides and four right angles: a rhombus and a rectangle.

cards.front_md: What is a kite?
cards.back_md: A 4-gon with two pairs of equal adjacent sides.

cards.front_md: List the properties of a parallelogram.
cards.back_md: Opposite sides equal, opposite angles equal, diagonals bisect each other.

cards.front_md: How do you prove opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal?
cards.back_md: Draw a diagonal; the two triangles are congruent by ASA (alternate angles); then CPCT.

cards.front_md: What do adjacent angles of a parallelogram add up to?
Name four tests for a parallelogram.
cards.back_md: Both pairs of opposite sides equal; both pairs of opposite angles equal; diagonals bisect each other; one pair of opposite sides equal and parallel.

cards.front_md: Is one pair of equal opposite sides enough for a parallelogram?
cards.back_md: No: an isosceles trapezium has a pair of equal opposite sides (the legs) and is not a parallelogram.

cards.front_md: What is special about the diagonals of a rhombus?
cards.back_md: They are perpendicular (and bisect each other).

cards.front_md: What is special about the diagonals of a rectangle?
cards.back_md: They are equal (and bisect each other).

cards.front_md: State the midpoint theorem.
cards.back_md: The segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half as long.

cards.front_md: How do you prove the midpoint theorem?
cards.back_md: Extend $DE$ to $F$ with $EF = DE$; $\triangle AED \cong \triangle CEF$ (SAS); $BDFC$ is a parallelogram.

cards.front_md: State the converse of the midpoint theorem.
cards.back_md: A line through the midpoint of one side parallel to a second side bisects the third side.

cards.front_md: Why is the converse of the midpoint theorem true?
cards.back_md: Only one line through the midpoint is parallel to the second side, and the line through the midpoint of the third side is one such line.

cards.front_md: What is the perimeter of the triangle formed by the midpoints of the sides?
cards.back_md: Half the perimeter of the original triangle.

cards.front_md: What is a median of a triangle?
cards.back_md: A segment from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.

cards.front_md: What does concurrent mean?
cards.back_md: Passing through one point.

cards.front_md: Where do the medians of a triangle meet, and in what ratio?
cards.back_md: At the centroid $G$, which divides each median in the ratio $2 : 1$ from the vertex.

cards.front_md: What 4-gon do the midpoints of the sides of any 4-gon form?
cards.back_md: A parallelogram (the Varignon parallelogram).

cards.front_md: Why is the midpoint 4-gon a parallelogram?
cards.back_md: Each of $PQ$ and $SR$ is parallel to the diagonal $AC$ and half of it, by the midpoint theorem.

cards.front_md: When is the midpoint 4-gon a rectangle? A rhombus?
cards.back_md: A rectangle when the diagonals are perpendicular; a rhombus when they are equal.

cards.front_md: How many lines of symmetry: rectangle, rhombus, kite, square, parallelogram?
Why does every 4-gon tile the plane?
cards.back_md: Four copies fit round a point using each angle once, since the angles add up to $360^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: Three angles of a tile in the shape of a 4-gon are $75^\circ$, $105^\circ$ and $85^\circ$. The fourth angle is
questions.solution_md: The angles of a 4-gon add up to $360^\circ$, so the fourth angle is $360^\circ - (75^\circ + 105^\circ + 85^\circ) = 95^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: The angles add up to $360^\circ$ and $2 + 3 + 4 + 6 = 15$ parts, so one part is $24^\circ$ and the largest angle is $6 \times 24 = 144^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: In a parallelogram $ABCD$, $\angle A = (5x - 20)^\circ$ and $\angle C = (3x + 30)^\circ$. The angle $\angle B$ is
questions.solution_md: Opposite angles are equal: $5x - 20 = 3x + 30$, so $x = 25$ and $\angle A = 105^\circ$. Adjacent angles add up to $180^\circ$, so $\angle B = 75^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal: $3x + 2 = 5x - 6$, so $x = 4$ and $AB = 3 \times 4 + 2 = 14$ m. The value $4$ is $x$.

questions.solution_md: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles, so a side is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with sides $8$ and $6$: $\sqrt{64 + 36} = 10$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Each side of $\triangle ADE$ is half of the matching side of $\triangle ABC$ ($AD = \frac12 AB$, $AE = \frac12 AC$, $DE = \frac12 BC$), so the perimeter of $\triangle ABC$ is $2 \times 18 = 36$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Each side of the triangle of midpoints is half of a side of the park, so the perimeter is half of $18 + 24 + 30 = 72$, that is $36$ m.

questions.stem_md: The diagonals of a 4-gon $ABCD$ are $12$ cm and $8$ cm. The 4-gon formed by joining the midpoints of its sides has perimeter
questions.solution_md: Its sides are parallel to the diagonals and half as long, so they are $6$ cm and $4$ cm, in two pairs. The perimeter is $2(6 + 4) = 20$ cm.

questions.stem_md: The diagonals of a 4-gon $ABCD$ are equal. The 4-gon formed by joining the midpoints of its sides is

options.text_md: a trapezium with only one pair of parallel sides

questions.solution_md: The midpoint 4-gon is a parallelogram whose sides are half of the diagonals, and the diagonals are equal, so all four of its sides are equal: it is a rhombus. It is a rectangle only if the diagonals are perpendicular, and a square only if they are both equal and perpendicular.

questions.stem_md: The midpoints of the sides of a rhombus (not a square) are joined in order. The 4-gon so formed is

questions.solution_md: The two diagonals of a rhombus are lines of symmetry, and there are no others unless it is a square. So there are $2$.

questions.stem_md: Prove that the angles of a 4-gon $ABCD$ add up to $360^\circ$. Three angles of a 4-gon-shaped plot are $85^\circ$, $100^\circ$ and $75^\circ$: find the fourth.

answer.model_answer_md:
Join the diagonal $AC$ inside the 4-gon. It makes $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle ACD$, each with angle sum $180^\circ$. The angles of the two triangles together make the four angles of $ABCD$, so the sum is $2 \times 180^\circ = 360^\circ$.

The fourth angle is $360^\circ - (85^\circ + 100^\circ + 75^\circ) = 100^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Two triangles, then subtract.

questions.stem_md: In a parallelogram $ABCD$, $\angle A = (4x - 10)^\circ$ and $\angle C = (2x + 30)^\circ$. Find $x$ and all four angles.

answer.model_answer_md:
Opposite angles are equal, so $4x - 10 = 2x + 30$, giving $x = 20$ and $\angle A = \angle C = 70^\circ$.

Adjacent angles add up to $180^\circ$, so $\angle B = \angle D = 180^\circ - 70^\circ = 110^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Opposite angles equal; adjacent angles supplementary.

marking_scheme.step: x = 20 and angles A and C 70 degrees

questions.stem_md: A rectangular gate of a school in Nashik is $12$ m wide and $5$ m high. A diagonal brace is fixed from one corner to the opposite corner. Find the length of the brace, and the distance from a corner to the point where the two diagonals cross.

answer.model_answer_md:
The brace is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle: $\sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13$ m.

The diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other, so the crossing point is $13 \div 2 = 6.5$ m from each corner.

questions.solution_md: Pythagoras, then halve.

marking_scheme.step: The distance 6.5 m, since the diagonals bisect each other

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle PQR$, $S$ and $T$ are the midpoints of $PQ$ and $PR$. $ST = 9.5$ cm and $\angle PST = 62^\circ$. Find $QR$ and $\angle PQR$, giving the reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
By the midpoint theorem $ST \parallel QR$ and $ST = \frac12 QR$, so $QR = 2 \times 9.5 = 19$ cm.

Since $ST \parallel QR$, the corresponding angles $\angle PST$ and $\angle PQR$ are equal, so $\angle PQR = 62^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Midpoint theorem, then corresponding angles.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $D$ is the midpoint of $AB$ and the line through $D$ parallel to $BC$ meets $AC$ at $E$. $DE = 7.2$ cm and $AC = 15.6$ cm. Find $BC$ and $AE$, naming the theorems used.

answer.model_answer_md:
By the converse of the midpoint theorem, $E$ is the midpoint of $AC$, so $AE = 15.6 \div 2 = 7.8$ cm.

By the midpoint theorem, $DE = \frac12 BC$, so $BC = 2 \times 7.2 = 14.4$ cm.

questions.stem_md: The diagonals of a 4-gon-shaped field $ABCD$ are $14$ m and $10$ m. The midpoints of its sides are joined in order. Name the figure formed and find its perimeter.

answer.model_answer_md:
The midpoints of the sides of any 4-gon form a **parallelogram**, whose sides are parallel to the diagonals and half as long: $7$ m and $5$ m.

Its perimeter is $2(7 + 5) = 24$ m.

questions.stem_md: Write the order of rotational symmetry, and the smallest angle of turn that makes the figure fit itself, for (i) a parallelogram that is not a rectangle or a rhombus, (ii) a square.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(i)** A parallelogram fits itself after a half-turn about the point where the diagonals meet: order $2$, smallest turn $180^\circ$.

**(ii)** A square fits itself after a quarter-turn: order $4$, smallest turn $360^\circ \div 4 = 90^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: In a 4-gon $ABCD$, $AB = DC$ and $AB \parallel DC$. Prove that $ABCD$ is a parallelogram. Check with $A(0, 0)$, $B(5, 0)$, $C(7, 2)$, $D(2, 2)$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Join $AC$. $\angle BAC = \angle ACD$ (alternate angles, $AB \parallel DC$), $AB = CD$ (given) and $AC = CA$ (common). So $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle CDA$ by SAS.

By CPCT $\angle ACB = \angle CAD$. These are alternate angles for $BC$ and $AD$, so $BC \parallel AD$. Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.

Check: $AB = DC = 5$ and $BC = AD = \sqrt{8}$.

questions.solution_md: SAS with the alternate angles, then CPCT.

marking_scheme.step: SAS for the triangles ABC and CDA
CPCT gives equal alternate angles, so BC is parallel to AD
Conclusion and the check AB = DC = 5

questions.stem_md: Prove that the diagonals of a rectangle $ABCD$ are equal. Check with $AB = 8$ cm and $BC = 6$ cm.

answer.model_answer_md:
In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DCB$: $AB = DC$ (opposite sides of a rectangle), $\angle ABC = \angle DCB = 90^\circ$ and $BC = CB$ (common).

So $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DCB$ by SAS, and $AC = DB$ by CPCT.

Check: $AC = BD = \sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = 10$ cm.

questions.solution_md: SAS with the right angles, then CPCT.

questions.stem_md: Prove that the diagonals of a rhombus $ABCD$ are perpendicular to each other. Check with diagonals $8$ cm and $6$ cm.

answer.model_answer_md:
The diagonals meet at $O$ and bisect each other (a rhombus is a parallelogram), so $OB = OD$. In $\triangle AOB$ and $\triangle AOD$: $AB = AD$ (sides of a rhombus), $OB = OD$ and $AO = AO$ (common).

So the triangles are congruent by SSS and $\angle AOB = \angle AOD$. They form a linear pair, so each is $90^\circ$.

Check: $AB = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5$ cm for all four sides.

questions.stem_md: In a parallelogram $ABCD$ the bisector of $\angle A$ meets $BC$ at $E$. Prove that $BE = AB$. Check with $AB = 4$ cm and $AD = 6$ cm, and find $EC$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\angle DAE = \angle BAE$ ($AE$ bisects $\angle A$). Since $AD \parallel BC$, $\angle DAE = \angle AEB$ (alternate angles). So $\angle BAE = \angle AEB$.

In $\triangle ABE$ the sides opposite equal angles are equal, so $BE = AB$.

Check: $BE = AB = 4$ cm and $BC = AD = 6$ cm, so $EC = 6 - 4 = 2$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Alternate angles make triangle ABE isosceles.

marking_scheme.step: Angle DAE = angle BAE, and angle DAE = angle AEB (alternate)
So BE = AB (equal angles, equal opposite sides)

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $D$, $E$, $F$ are the midpoints of $BC$, $CA$, $AB$. Prove that the four triangles $AFE$, $FBD$, $EDC$ and $DEF$ are congruent. Check with $AB = 10$, $BC = 12$, $CA = 14$ cm.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so $O$ is the midpoint of $AC$ and of $BD$: $OB = OD$.

**(b)** $OP = OB - BP$ and $OQ = OD - DQ$. Since $OB = OD$ and $BP = DQ$, $OP = OQ$.

**(c)** $O$ is the midpoint of $AC$ and also of $PQ$, so the diagonals $AC$ and $PQ$ of $APCQ$ bisect each other.

**(d)** A 4-gon whose diagonals bisect each other is a parallelogram, so $APCQ$ is a parallelogram.

**(e)** $O = (4, 1.5)$ is the midpoint of $AC$, and of $PQ$ with $P = (5, 0.75)$ and $Q = (3, 2.25)$.

children.solution_md: The two diagonals of a rhombus are its lines of symmetry. It has $4$ only if it is a square.
